lessons.title: Credit Policy: Deciding Who Gets Credit, How Much and For How Long

children.text: Credit is a product your business gives away for free, in unlimited quantities, to whoever asks. That is what an undocumented credit policy amounts to. The sales team decides terms deal by deal, nobody tracks the total exposure to any one customer, and the finance team finds out when a payment is 90 days late.
A
credit policy
answers four questions in advance: who gets credit, how much, for how long, and what happens when they break the terms. This lesson covers the first three. The fourth belongs to the next lesson.

markDefs.definition: The written rules deciding which customers get credit, how much, for how long, and what happens when they do not pay on time.

children.text: Question One: Who Gets Credit
Every customer should be graded before the first invoice goes out, and regraded at least once a year. The inputs are easier to get in India than most people assume.

body.title: What to actually ask for, and what to check yourself

children.text: Ask the customer for: the last two years of audited financial statements, the last six months of GST returns, the last six months of bank statements, and two trade references from their existing suppliers. A customer who refuses all four is telling you something useful.

Check yourself: the company master data and charge filings on the Ministry of Corporate Affairs portal, which show whether the entity is active, whether accounts have been filed on time, and what assets are already charged to lenders. Pull a commercial credit bureau report where you can. Search for insolvency proceedings, because an application admitted against a customer changes everything about your exposure.

The GST returns matter more than most sellers realise. Comparing the sales the customer declares in its returns with the scale of credit it is asking from you is a fast reality check, and consistent delays in filing are an early sign of cash strain.

body.title: The five Cs, in an Indian context

cards.definition: Payment track record with you and with the trade references. Ask other suppliers in the same market, since reputations travel fast in a trade cluster.
Whether the cash flows support the exposure. Read the GST returns and bank statements, not just the profit figure.
The owner's own money in the business. A thinly capitalised buyer passes its risk straight to you.
Security you can fall back on: a bank guarantee, letter of credit, security deposit or personal guarantee.
The state of the customer's own industry and its customers. A supplier to a stressed sector inherits that stress.

cells: Listed or large corporate, clean payment record over two years
Established business, occasional delays within 15 days of due date
Personal guarantee of the proprietor or directors
Security deposit, or bank guarantee for larger orders
Disputes, cheque returns, or repeated delays beyond 45 days

body.text: The grade should drive the terms automatically, and the sales team should know the grid. The argument you want to avoid is the one where every deal becomes a separate negotiation about credit, settled by whoever pushes hardest in the room.

children.text: Question Two: How Much
A credit limit per customer is the single most effective control in the whole policy, because it caps the damage from any one failure. Size it from how the customer actually buys.

body.caption: Sized so that a customer buying normally never trips the limit

children.text: A dealer buying ₹40 lakh a month on 45-day terms carries a natural exposure of about ₹60 lakh. Add a 20% buffer for festive season bulk orders and the limit is ₹72 lakh. Anything beyond that requires a specific approval, ideally with additional security rather than a verbal assurance.

stats.label: Sanctioned limit
stats.context: With a 20% buffer for seasonal peaks

stats.label: Above the limit
stats.context: Bank guarantee, letter of credit or advance payment

body.text: A credit limit that is never enforced is not a limit. The control has to sit in the system that releases the dispatch, not in a policy document. If the sales team can ship to a customer who is over limit or overdue without a documented approval, you do not have a credit policy.

children.text: Question Three: How Long

Lengthening credit terms is a commercial decision with an arithmetic answer. A Nashik packaging company currently sells ₹120 crore a year on 30-day terms. Sales estimates that moving to 60 days would lift sales by 12%, to ₹134.4 crore. Contribution margin is 25%, so variable cost is 75% of sales, the business funds receivables at 10%, and bad debts would rise from 0.5% of sales to 1.2%.

body.caption: Incremental analysis of the credit extension (₹ crore)

cells: Investment in receivables at variable cost

children.text: The proposal adds ₹1.67 crore of profit, so it is worth doing. Notice what makes it work: the extra contribution of ₹3.6 crore comfortably exceeds the ₹0.92 crore of financing cost and the ₹1.01 crore of extra bad debt combined. Notice also which number is fragile.

body.title: What the credit extension gives and takes (₹ crore)

body.label: The number to stress test
body.context: At 2.44% the entire gain disappears. The financing cost is predictable, but the bad debt assumption is a guess, and it is the one that decides the answer.

body.text: Always compute the investment in receivables at variable cost, not at invoice value. The profit margin inside an unpaid invoice was never cash you had, so financing it costs you nothing. Using the full invoice value overstates the cost of extending credit and kills proposals that are actually worth doing.

body.title: Run the analysis yourself
body.prompt: A company sells ₹100 crore a year on 30-day terms. Moving to 45 days is expected to lift sales 8%, to ₹108 crore. Contribution margin is 30%, so variable cost is 70% of sales. Receivables are funded at 11%. Bad debts would rise from 0.8% of sales to 1.5%. What is the net effect on profit, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: Extra contribution is ₹8 crore times 30%, which is ₹2.4 crore. Receivables rise from ₹8.219 crore to ₹13.315 crore, so the extra investment at variable cost is ₹3.57 crore, costing ₹0.39 crore at 11%. Bad debts rise from ₹0.8 crore to ₹1.62 crore, an increase of ₹0.82 crore. The net gain is ₹1.19 crore, so the extension pays, though less comfortably than the first example.

children.text: Getting Paid Without Giving Credit
Before accepting risk, check whether you can transfer it. Indian sellers have more options here than they typically use.

body.title: Ways to reduce the credit you actually carry

columns.label: Security and instruments
points: Advance or part advance, standard for new customers
Security deposit from dealers, adjusted against the final invoice
Bank guarantee for large or lumpy exposures
Letter of credit, which converts customer risk into bank risk
Electronic mandates under NACH for recurring collections

columns.label: Financing routes
points: Channel financing, where the bank funds your dealers and pays you upfront
Invoice discounting on a TReDS platform when the buyer is a large corporate
Credit insurance, including ECGC cover for export receivables
Early payment discounts, which buy back your own cash at a stated price

children.text: Two of these deserve emphasis. A
letter of credit
moves the risk from a customer you cannot assess to a bank you can. And
channel financing

is how most large Indian manufacturers keep their own receivable days low while their dealers still get credit: the bank funds the dealer, the manufacturer gets paid on dispatch. Chapter 6 covers these in detail.

markDefs.definition: Letter of credit. A bank undertaking to pay the seller if the buyer does not, converting customer risk into bank risk.
An arrangement where a bank funds a manufacturer's dealers directly, so the manufacturer is paid upfront while the dealer repays the bank later.

body.text: Post-dated cheques are still common in Indian trade, but treat them as a discipline tool rather than security. Recovery through a dishonoured cheque case takes years, and the cheque is worth nothing if the account is empty. Electronic mandates under NACH are cleaner, and a bank guarantee is real security.

body.title: The right cost base
body.textWithBlank: When measuring the cost of carrying receivables, the investment should be valued at ___ cost rather than at invoice value, because the profit margin inside an unpaid invoice was never cash the business had.
body.explanation: Using variable cost keeps the analysis honest. Valuing receivables at invoice value overstates the carrying cost and can make a profitable credit extension look like a loss.

body.title: Where does the analysis break?
body.question: In the packaging company example, which assumption most deserves a stress test before approving the longer credit terms?
options: The funding rate of 10%, since interest rates move
The bad debt rate of 1.2%, since the extra sales come from customers the company has not dealt with before
The contribution margin of 25%, since it is fixed by the product mix
The 365-day divisor used to convert sales into receivables
body.explanation: The financing cost is small and predictable, and the margin is known. The bad debt rate is an estimate about customers who are new, and it is precisely the marginal customers attracted by longer credit who default most often. At 2.44% of sales the entire gain is wiped out.

body.title: The festive season limit request
body.scenario: It is September. Your largest dealer in Indore has a ₹72 lakh credit limit and currently owes ₹68 lakh, of which ₹9 lakh is 20 days past due. He asks for the limit to be raised to ₹1.2 crore for the festive season, promising to clear everything by mid-December. He has been a customer for six years, has never actually defaulted, and accounts for about 11% of your sales. The sales head supports the request strongly.
body.prompt: How would you decide, and what would you offer?
body.modelAnswer:
Do not treat this as a yes or no question. Treat it as a pricing and security question.

Start with the facts. Six years without a default is worth a lot, but the ₹9 lakh past due matters more than the history: the existing limit is already being breached in substance. Eleven per cent of sales means losing him hurts, and it also means a single failure would be a serious hit. Both facts point the same way, which is that this exposure deserves structure rather than trust.

What to offer. First, clear the overdue ₹9 lakh before any enhancement, as a condition rather than a request. Second, grant the increase as a temporary seasonal limit with a hard expiry date in December, not a permanent revision, so it lapses automatically. Third, ask for security on the incremental ₹48 lakh: a bank guarantee, a letter of credit, or post-dated electronic mandates staggered through November and December. Fourth, check whether your bank offers channel financing, which is the clean answer here, since the dealer gets his festive credit from the bank and you get paid on dispatch.

What to watch. Track the exposure weekly through the season rather than monthly, and stop further dispatches automatically if the limit or the ageing is breached. Set that rule now, in writing, while everyone is happy. It is far harder to impose in December.

body.title: What a written credit policy should contain
steps: A customer grading method, with the specific documents required at onboarding.
Standard credit terms by grade, and the approval level needed to deviate from them.
A credit limit for every customer, reviewed at least annually and enforced in the dispatch system.
Security requirements by grade and by exposure size.
The rule for temporary seasonal limits, including their automatic expiry.
The specific trigger that stops dispatches, such as any amount over 30 days past due.
Who owns collections, and the escalation timetable covered in the next lesson.
A rule that the incremental analysis must be run before any general change in terms.

body.label: Check a customer on the MCA portal
body.description: Company master data shows whether an entity is active and filing on time, and the index of charges shows which of its assets are already pledged to lenders. Both are free and take minutes before you approve a large exposure.

body.text: Credit is a loan your business makes without an interest rate, a repayment schedule or a credit committee. Give it the same discipline a bank would, or accept that you are pricing a loan at zero and hoping.

points: A credit policy answers four questions in advance: who gets credit, how much, for how long, and what happens when terms are broken.
Grade customers before the first invoice, using audited accounts, GST returns, bank statements, trade references and MCA filings.
Set a credit limit for every customer, sized from normal monthly purchases and the credit period, with a buffer for seasonal peaks.
A limit only works if it is enforced in the system that releases dispatches, not in a policy document.
Decide changes in credit terms with incremental analysis: extra contribution against carrying cost plus extra bad debt.
Value the investment in receivables at variable cost, not invoice value, or you will reject proposals that are worth doing.
The bad debt assumption is usually the fragile one, because longer terms attract exactly the customers most likely to default.
Before carrying customer risk, check whether a bank guarantee, letter of credit, channel financing or credit insurance can transfer it.
